## Intent
Hypothesis: scalar per-particle execution with the death verdict kept in registers can avoid intermediate-storage overhead and remain competitive against vectorized variants through sequential AoS streaming.

## Layout & approach
The 68 B/particle AoS layout offers 32 hot bytes per particle to loop 1 (age+pos+seed+vel, 47% of the line) and 28 hot bytes to loop 2 (color+pos, 41%); the remaining 53–59% is dead weight dragged through every cache line. With no intermediate storage, the death verdict stays in registers, eliminating a second pass over particle data. The approach is purely scalar — branchy respawn via conditional jumps and byte-granular color scatter — so the dead-byte fraction matters less than it would for a streaming kernel, because this code never approaches streaming bandwidth. The working set spills L1d at N≈481, L2 at N≈7710, and L3 at N≈246723, but the flatness of the cost curve across these transitions (below) shows the layout's cache behavior is not the governing constraint.

## Cache saturation
At q=0.01 the cost rises only from 22.1 ns/p (L1d-resident, N=320) to 25.5 ns/p (DRAM, N=10M) — a 15% increase across the entire hierarchy, with no visible knee at the L1d→L2 spill (N≈481) or the L2→L3 spill (N≈7710). The L3-resident band (N=10000–160000) is flat at ~24–25 ns/p, and the DRAM band (N=250000+) is equally flat. This shape confirms the algo is not memory-bound: the 47% hot fraction and 68 B stride would produce a spill knee only if the code streamed, but it does not. At q=0.5 the cost is ~33–34 ns/p at every N regardless of regime — death rate, not cache residency, sets the cost. The dense grid resolves no knee because there is none to resolve.

## Bandwidth
Achieved bandwidth is 2.0–3.1 GB/s against the 12.69 GB/s ceiling — 16–24% of ceiling. The memory floor is 5.359 ns/p; this algo runs at 22–34 ns/p, 4–6× above the floor, so the vast majority of time is not irreducible memory time. The verdict is frontend-bound, not bandwidth-bound: backend stalls are 0.0% and branch flushes are 0.0% across all profiles, while frontend stalls consume 64–70%. The 1.0× baseline ratio at every point confirms this IS the baseline. Against the winner (AF02.LP1-autovec.LP2-opt), the gap is 2.0× at q=0.5/N=320 (33.6 vs ~16.8 ns/p) and widens to 3.6× at q=0.01/N=160000 (24.4 vs ~6.8 ns/p) — the autovec winner extracts ILP that scalar code cannot, and the gap is largest where death rate is lowest and compute density matters most.

## Assembly
The codegen is entirely scalar FP: `vmovss`, `vmulss`, `vaddss` for all arithmetic (22 scalar FP ops in loop 1, 14 in loop 2) and `vucomiss` for comparisons. Only 4 vector-suffixed instructions appear in 360 (`vxorps`, `vmovd`) — no auto-vectorization occurred. No gathers are present; AoS fields are accessed at fixed offsets within the 68 B stride (`[rbx]`, `[rbx+0xc]`, `[rbx+0x10]`, etc.). Loop 1 carries 14 conditional branches with branchy respawn (`jae`→spawn path at L59, `jne`/`je` chains for death checks). Loop 2 uses `cmovae`-based select clamping with 21 cond-branches and byte-granular scatter (`movzx` + `mov BYTE PTR [r13+r14*1+0x0]` for RGB writes). The 118 insns/iter (loop 1) and 195 insns/iter (loop 2) explain the 65–70% frontend stall: the decode pipeline cannot supply enough μops per cycle, leaving compute at only 30–36% of cycles.

## Verdict
Refuted — 1.0× of naive at every point (it IS the baseline) and 2.0–3.6× slower than the winner everywhere. At q=0.01/N=160000 it is 3.6× slower than the autovec winner (24.4 vs ~6.8 ns/p); at q=0.5/N=320 it is still 2.0× slower (33.6 vs ~16.8 ns/p). The mechanism is frontend starvation: 118–195 scalar instructions per iteration with 14–21 conditional branches hold achieved bandwidth at 16–24% of ceiling and 4–6× above the memory floor, while the register-resident verdict and lack of intermediates cannot compensate for the total absence of vectorization.
